title: Train on your own output. What's lost?
hook: Each model learns from the last one's words. Can a rare word survive?

knows: that models learn word frequencies from data
that a model's output can end up in the next model's training data
doesNotKnow: that retraining on a model's own samples loses rare things permanently

misconception: Averaging over many samples preserves the distribution.
objective: The learner can explain that each generation trained on samples of the last can only lose rare items, never regain them, so a loop of models trained on model output narrows.

claims.text: A word that is 2% of the data is missed by all 50 draws with chance 0.98^50 = 36.4%, about one run in three; in this toy, once its count is 0 it can never be drawn again.
claims.source: Independent draws: (1 − 0.02)^50 = 0.3642. Absorption at 0 follows from drawing only from current frequencies (nextGen in Demo.tsx). exactLoss(50) in Demo.tsx. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): node: 0.98^50 = 0.36417 -> 36.4% (reveal toFixed(1)); own Monte Carlo (Math.random, 200,000 trials) 36.3%; own reimplementation of nextGen with kit mulberry32, runs 1-2000: zebra lost in generation 1 in 37.3%. The sampler skips zero counts, and in 2000 x 10 generations no zero count ever came back.

claims.text: With 500 draws per generation the 2% word is lost in one generation with chance 0.98^500 ≈ 0.004%, but in the toy losses still only accumulate: bigger samples slow the losing, they do not undo it.
claims.source: exactLoss(500) = 4.1e-5 in Demo.tsx; lossRate(500, 2000) = 0 in 2,000 seeded runs. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): node: 0.98^500 = 4.10e-5 = 0.0041%, 'about 0.004%' right. Runs 1-2000 at 500 draws: zebra lost in generation 1 in 0 runs; words left after 10 generations average 9.61 of 10 (vs 5.35 at 50 draws); no zero ever revived. Slows, does not undo: holds.

claims.text: The toy resamples word counts only; it has no real model, and the ten words are invented.
claims.source: Brief 30 in company/domains/briefs/ai.md; labelled on the stage and in the reveal.

claims.text: Real models trained recursively on model-generated data lose the rare cases (the tails of the distribution) first.
claims.source: About real systems: Shumailov et al. 2024, 'AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data', Nature 631, 755-759. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Shumailov et al. 2024, Nature 631:755-759 confirmed; abstract says tails of the original distribution disappear.

recall.question: In this closed resampling model, each generation learns only from the previous generation’s output. What can happen to rare subjects?
options: Some can disappear and cannot return without new data
They stay as common as they were, on average
They become more common, because models like variety
recall.why: In this model, a rare subject can miss a round by chance. Once its count reaches zero, no later sample can restore it; fresh data would change that assumption.
